questions.question: D3 — SQL injection in user lookup: the plan uses request.params.userId directly in a raw SQL fragment. The plan itself notes this string is not sanitized. How should the plan be fixed? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-sql-injection>

options.label: 3A: Parameterized query (Recommended)
options.description: Replace the raw SQL fragment with a parameterized query binding userId to a $1 placeholder. Eliminates SQL injection entirely. The plan's 'existing contracts retained' section already acknowledges the string is unsafe for SQL — the fix is a one-liner. Verify: unit test with userId = '1 OR 1=1' asserts the handler rejects/escapes it, not executes it. Completeness: 10/10.

options.label: 3B: Input validation before SQL
options.description: Validate userId is a positive integer before the DB call; reject the webhook with HTTP 400 if invalid. Adds defense-in-depth but is not sufficient alone (validation can be bypassed; parameterized queries cannot). Use alongside 3A, not instead of it. Completeness: 7/10 if standalone.

options.label: 3C: Do nothing — accept the risk
options.description: Leave the raw SQL as-is. The Stripe signature verification reduces (but does not eliminate) the attack surface. Not recommended: any actor who can craft a Stripe payment intent with a malicious metadata.user_id can trigger this, including test-mode API keys or compromised merchant accounts. Completeness: 3/10.

questions.question: D4 — The plan has zero tests for a payment-critical handler. How should this be addressed? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-tests>

options.label: 4A: Full test suite (Recommended)
options.description: Add unit tests for the handler (happy path, missing user, injected userId, email failure) AND one integration test that replays a real Stripe payload through the full stack and asserts user record updated + email logged. With CC this takes ~15 minutes to implement. This is the test you'd need to ship at 2am on a Friday. Completeness: 10/10.

options.label: 4B: Smoke tests only
options.description: Add 2 smoke tests: one happy-path integration test, one for the SQL injection guard. Skips edge cases (email failure, missing user, N+1 regression). Faster but leaves gaps. Completeness: 6/10.

options.label: 4C: Defer to existing integration suite
options.description: Keep the plan as-is: rely on the existing integration suite to catch regressions. The plan states this explicitly. Risk: the existing suite likely doesn’t know about this new handler’s specific failure modes (SQL injection, email failure cascade, N+1). Not recommended. Completeness: 3/10.

questions.question: D5 — Email send fires inline with no error handling. A provider timeout holds the transaction lock and returns 500 to Stripe (triggering retries). How should this be fixed? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-email-error>

options.label: 5A: Try/catch with structured logging (Recommended)
options.description: Wrap the email call in try/catch. On failure: log structured error (userId, eventId, error class), and return 200 — the payment succeeded; the email is non-fatal. Add an explicit timeout to the email call (e.g., 5s) so provider slowness doesn’t hold the transaction lock. Verify: unit test asserts handler returns 200 when email throws. Completeness: 9/10.

options.label: 5B: Async email via job queue
options.description: Enqueue an email job instead of sending inline. The webhook returns 200 immediately after the DB update; email delivery is decoupled and retried independently. Fully resilient but adds a job queue dependency (may already exist). Completeness: 10/10, but larger scope change.

options.label: 5C: Leave inline, no error handling
options.description: Keep email send inline with no catch. Accept that email provider failures will cause 500s and Stripe retries. The dedup guard should prevent duplicate DB updates on retry (if transaction scope is correct). Not recommended: silent email failures are never acceptable in a payment flow. Completeness: 3/10.

questions.question: D6 — The plan fetches orders in a per-order loop (N+1 queries). Under concurrent webhook volume this exhausts DB connections. How should this be fixed? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-n1-query>

options.label: 6A: Single batch query (Recommended)
options.description: Replace the per-order loop with one parameterized batch query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1. Reduces O(N) queries to O(1). Verify: confirm an index exists on orders.user_id; if not, add one in the same migration. Assert in tests that only 3 DB queries fire per webhook (lookup, batch orders, update). Completeness: 10/10.

options.label: 6B: Keep the loop, add a DB index
options.description: Keep the per-order fetch loop but ensure an index exists on orders.user_id. Reduces full-table scans but doesn’t eliminate the N+1 round-trips. Still O(N) queries. Completeness: 6/10.

options.label: 6C: Accept as-is, defer optimization
options.description: Leave the N+1 loop and note it as a known performance issue for later. Acceptable only if order counts per user are guaranteed to be very low (e.g., ≤5) AND webhook volume is low. The plan gives no such guarantee. Completeness: 3/10.

questions.question:
D1 — Which implementation approach for processPayment() test coverage?

ELI10: The plan specifies exactly 2 unit tests: happy path (Stripe succeeds → receipt generated) and 502-exhaustion (Stripe 502 → retry once → clean failure). A third natural scenario exists — retry-then-success (Stripe 502 → retry → Stripe succeeds → correct receipt) — which the adapter suite already models but processPayment() has no unit test for. The question is how much test coverage to write while you're in the code.

Stakes if we pick wrong: Too narrow leaves the retry-then-success orchestration untested, risking silent regressions on the recovery path. Too wide duplicates adapter-suite coverage without adding new signal.

Recommendation: B because it closes the one genuinely missing orchestration scenario for ~10 extra lines, without duplicating adapter-boundary tests.

Completeness: A=7/10, B=9/10, C=10/10 (C has diminishing returns due to 402/429 adapter overlap)

<gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-approach>

options.label: B) Standard — 3 tests (Recommended)
options.description: Add the 2 specified tests plus a third: retry-then-success (502 → retry → charge succeeds → correct receipt). Uses the same infrastructure the adapter suite already uses for this scenario. Effort: human ~40 min / CC ~3 min. Completeness: 9/10.

options.label: A) Minimal — exactly 2 tests as specified
options.description: Happy path + 502-exhaustion only. Smallest possible diff, zero scope creep, uses existing factory/sleeper. The retry-then-success path remains untested at processPayment() level. Effort: human ~30 min / CC ~2 min. Completeness: 7/10.

options.label: C) Full — 5 tests (all Stripe outcomes)
options.description: Happy path, 502-exhaust, retry-then-success, 402 decline, 429 rate-limit — all tested at the processPayment() level. Maximum confidence; eliminates all coverage questions permanently. Risk: 402/429 may duplicate adapter-suite tests without new signal. Effort: human ~75 min / CC ~5 min. Completeness: 10/10.

questions.question:
D2 — Which review mode for this test coverage plan?

ELI10: Approach B is locked in (3 tests: happy path, 502-exhaust, retry-then-success). The review mode decides HOW rigorously I examine that scope. HOLD SCOPE means I focus entirely on making those 3 tests bulletproof — catching every ambiguity about what to assert, how to name tests, what 'fails clean' means, edge cases in the retry path. SELECTIVE EXPANSION means I do that rigorous review AND surface cherry-pick opportunities like additional structural improvements or assertion depth upgrades.

Stakes if we pick wrong: Too expansive turns a simple 3-test addition into a bigger refactor. Too narrow misses critical specification gaps (what exactly should be asserted in each test).

Recommendation: HOLD SCOPE because the plan is already well-scoped at 3 tests; the highest value is making those tests precise — specifying exact assertions, defining 'fails clean', confirming backoff is asserted and not just recorded.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

<gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-mode>

options.label: HOLD SCOPE (Recommended)
options.description: Take the 3-test scope as final. Review with maximum rigor: catch every assertion gap, specify what 'fails clean' means, validate the backoff assertion, define the receipt fields under test. Make each test bulletproof before implementation starts.

options.label: SELECTIVE EXPANSION
options.description: Hold the 3-test baseline AND surface cherry-pick opportunities: e.g., test naming conventions, shared setup helpers, assertion libraries, or a 4th edge case. Each expansion is individually opt-in. More expansive but still user-controlled.

options.label: SCOPE REDUCTION
options.description: Pull back to the original 2 tests (drop retry-then-success). Strictest possible minimum. Only if you feel approach B overshot.

questions.question:
D3 — Section 2: Should the plan specify the error contract for "fails clean"?

ELI10: The 502-exhaustion test needs to assert something specific when processPayment() gives up after one retry. The plan says it should "fail clean" but doesn't say what that means in code: does processPayment() raise a named exception (e.g. PaymentGatewayError), return nil, or return an error result object? Without this, the implementer might write an assertion that passes trivially — for instance, asserting that the return value is nil when the function actually raises, meaning the rescue path is never exercised.

Stakes if we pick wrong: An underspecified assertion could let a broken retry path pass the test silently.

Recommendation: A — add a one-line note to the plan naming the error contract ("processPayment() raises X" or "returns nil"), so the test asserts the right thing. This is one sentence of spec, not implementation work.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

<gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-fails-clean>

options.label: A) Add spec: name the error contract (Recommended)
options.description: Add a brief note to the plan specifying what processPayment() does on retry exhaustion (raises SpecificError / returns nil / returns error object). Implementer then asserts the correct thing. One sentence.

options.label: B) Leave as-is: implementer reads the source
options.description: The production code already has a defined behavior. The implementer will look at processPayment() and write the correct assertion without the plan needing to spell it out.

answers.D3 \u2014 Section 2: Should the plan spe: A) Add spec: name the error contract (Recommended)

questions.question:
D4 — Section 6: Should the plan explicitly require asserting Stripe call count for retry tests?

ELI10: The 502-exhaustion test and the retry-then-success test both involve a retry. The plan says the test should "assert retry-with-backoff fires once" — but without explicitly asserting the Stripe call count (expect 2 calls via mock call history), a broken implementation that skips the retry entirely would still pass if it produces the right final outcome. The factory already exposes the mock call history, so this assertion costs one line per test.

Stakes if we pick wrong: Skip it — a future refactor that accidentally removes the retry logic could pass both tests if it happens to produce the same final failure/receipt. Add it — the tests are more brittle (they now break if retry count changes) but correctly verify the retry behavior.

Recommendation: A — the plan explicitly states "retry-with-backoff fires once," which implies the retry count IS the behavior under test. Asserting it makes that intent machine-verifiable. One line per test, already free via factory.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

<gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-retry-count>

options.label: A) Add to plan: assert Stripe call count in both retry tests (Recommended)
options.description: The 502-exhaustion and retry-then-success tests should each assert the exact Stripe call count (2) via the mock call history. One line per test. Verifies the retry actually executed, not just the final outcome.

options.label: B) Leave as-is: assert outcome only
options.description: Tests assert the final state (failure/receipt) only. Retry behavior is tested at the adapter suite level. Simpler tests, but a retry regression could pass silently.

answers.D4 \u2014 Section 6: Should the plan exp: A) Add to plan: assert Stripe call count in both retry tests (Recommended)
